items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-10-26
items.q: But he tried to build his style the same as Napoleon, Red Norval, Red Nichols.

ctx.x: I think he said this, hadn't he, somewhere? Yes. He said he studied your records?

Yes. That's all he ever knew was original Dixieland jazz band music. But he tried to build his style the same as Napoleon, Red Norval, Red Nichols. All these fellas tried to make up a different style of their own, to be a little different. They added to it, and what it is today, it ain't what we played. It's nowhere near it, because you can listen to our records. I don't say we great musicians, but we only knew playing harmony. Today they use more modern harmony, and they got better technique, and they taught in…
I've known people who had classical training who never could learn to play jazz.

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-16
items.q: I remember when Philly Napoleon came to me around 1918, he used to beg me to show him how to make slurs in different passages on the clarinet.

ctx.x: Well, we forgot about Lytel and Frankie Signorelli. About 1920, Signorelli joined my band. At that time they may have had a Memphis Five, but I never heard of them stopping the machine. Well, I had a little bit of friction with Roberson. He had promised the band a thousand dollars if I put Margie over. Well, I saw the plug of Margie for him, sang it for him, placed it on the record for him, and after he got his first statement, he didn't say anything. I asked him about what he was going to do to three of them.…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-02
items.q: He wanted Philly Napoleon and Johnny Costello and men that knew the Dixieland style of music.

ctx.x: I forgot certain incidents at places like we played in London before we came back to America. We were asked by the British government to play at the Savoy Hotel. That was a celebration of the Peace Victory Ball. Yeah we worked to play the dance music and we went on over there after they had all the parades and all kinds of ceremonies in the street all day. People were kissing one another. Men were even kissing you on the street. They were so happy. That night we went over to the Savoy Hotel and we mounted the…

Yes that's right. We'll keep it now. This is a letter from Emil Christian and it says I would like Philip Napoleon on cornet and Johnny Costello on clarinet. The boys I was working with because they have more of an idea what I want and they can play all the Dixieland numbers because I'll know we'll get some requests for them. It's signed on the back here.
